title: Similarities and differences in anthropometry and training between recreational male 100-km ultra-marathoners and marathoners
authors: Rüst CA, Knechtle B, Knechtle P, Rosemann T
population: 166 recreational male 100-km ultra-marathoners and 126 male marathoners.
findings: Marathoners completed fewer hours and fewer km per week (both P < 0.001) but ran faster in training (P < 0.001).
In the 100-km runners, weekly running kilometres were negatively related to race time (P < 0.0001); age (P < 0.0001), body mass (P = 0.011) and body fat (P = 0.019) were positively related.
In marathoners, body fat (P = 0.002) was positively and training speed (P < 0.0001) negatively associated with marathon time.
Authors conclude ultra-marathoners rely on volume in running training, marathoners on speed.
limitations: Cross-sectional, self-reported training, men only, performance outcome only, no longest-run or back-to-back variable in the abstract.
implications: Supports weekly volume as the main performance lever for 100 km, which argues against capping weekly load to make room for a very long single run.
Says nothing about the longest single run, so it cannot validate a 240 min target.

verification.notes: Re-fetched Crossref (J Sports Sci, 2012-06-25, Rüst) and Europe PMC abstract (PMID 22724447). N and all P values match; full author list added.
